paras: The threatened lynching of Dan Ritchie took place in Ashland, Wisconsin, early on August 30, 1888, when a crowd of railroad men gathered intending to take the saloonkeeper from the county jail and lynch him for the shooting of switchman William Amrine. The crowd, reported at nearly 200 men, dispersed after Sheriff Breen warned that armed deputies inside would shoot to kill, and the wire story that carried the news across the country praised him as an example to other sheriffs.

According to an August 29 dispatch, Amrine, a switchman for the Wisconsin Central road, and Ritchie had a "misunderstanding while intoxicated" at about 3 a.m. that day at Ritchie's saloon in the "Bay City" district. Ritchie reportedly knocked Amrine down and stamped on his face, after which two policemen separated the men and put Amrine into the street, where he threw a handful of gravel through the window. Ritchie then reportedly ran out with a revolver and fired five shots at the retreating Amrine, hitting him in the back of the head and in the hip. A coroner's jury returned a verdict "in accordance with the facts," Ritchie was jailed, and railroad men talked during the day of lynching him.

At about 1 a.m. on August 30, dispatches from Ashland reported a crowd of "angry men" gathered near a trestle bridge west of the Central railway yards, expected to rush the new jail and drag Ritchie out. The sheriff, deputies and police held the jail, though a railroad man in the crowd said they would not be fired on. A later wire report said the crowd gathered within a few blocks of the jail and waited for a signal to rush it. When Sheriff Breen told the men that twelve deputies inside would "shoot to kill" anyone who tried to enter, the crowd dispersed because, in the dispatch's words, no one "of sufficient courage" could be found to lead it.

The threat did not end there: on August 31 the St. Paul Daily Globe reported that railroad men had met and formed a "regulators' committee," and that railroaders from other lines had come in. Breen again posted ten armed deputies in the jail, and the Globe judged the situation "more threatening" than it had been on Thursday morning. No second move on the jail was reported, and Ritchie remained in jail.

Ritchie was committed for trial on the afternoon of August 30, and Amrine's body was shipped to Kappa, Illinois, that night. Examined before Justice Metgher on a murder charge, he was bound over. On September 13 Amrine's father, Dexter Amrine of Kappa, came to the jail and told Ritchie that he wanted "to see the man who murdered my son"; the Globe said he had come to see "proper punishment" meted out. Ritchie was arraigned in circuit court on December 4, and Judge Parish granted him a continuance until the next term. No report of a trial, or of any arrest of the crowd, was found.

The St. Paul Daily Globe followed the case through specials from Ashland under headlines such as "Strong Talk of Lynching" and "He May Be Hemped." Its first report called Amrine "Maltreated and Murdered" and the beating a "brutal punishment," and its August 31 special gave the mob's view that the sheriff would not shoot them to save a man "who shot one of their companions in the back."

The Rock Island Argus headed the wire story "An Example for Sheriffs" and closed it by saying the sheriff's "determined stand saved the prisoner from a terrible fate." Other papers ran the same text as "Lynchers Lost Courage" in Accomac, Virginia, and "Determined Sheriff Balks a Mob" in Macon, Mississippi, and also in Washington, Wilmington and Maysville. In mid-September Wisconsin weeklies in River Falls and Kenosha carried it as "A Plucky Sheriff."
Every version called Ritchie "the murderer" of Amrine before any trial, and none stated the race of anyone involved.

The papers differed on Amrine's family: the Globe's first report said he left "a widowed monther [mother] at Bloomington, Ill.," while its later dispatches sent his body to Kappa, Illinois, and described a visit from his father, Dexter Amrine of Kappa.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Dan Ritchie
bases: A crowd gathered near the Ashland jail to take Dan Ritchie out and lynch him for killing William Amrine, and dispersed when the sheriff threatened to fire (A1, A2, A5); coded as a threatened lynching.

A crowd of nearly 200 meant to take Ritchie from jail and lynch him for a killing (A5, A1), a group acting without legal authority on a pretext of justice, but it dispersed and no one was killed (A5, A13).

The Globe's Ashland specials (A2, A8) and the separate national wire story (A5, reprinted in A3, A6, A7, A10, A11) agree that a crowd gathered to lynch Ritchie and was held off by the sheriff, though they may share one Ashland correspondent.

framing.detail: The St. Paul Daily Globe headlined the lynching prospect ('Strong Talk of Lynching', 'He May Be Hemped') and called the beating of Amrine 'brutal'.
The wire story, headed 'An Example for Sheriffs' and 'A Plucky Sheriff', praised the sheriff's stand for saving the prisoner from 'a terrible fate'.
Papers in Washington, Wilmington, Maysville, Macon, Accomac, River Falls and Middleburgh ran the wire text, some under headlines such as 'Lynchers Lost Courage'.
